pedagogy.summary: Fraction notation (a/b) is a compact language: the denominator names how many equal parts one whole is split into, the numerator counts how many of those parts we have — and the two together name a SINGLE number, not two separate whole numbers. Teach the vocabulary in use, always anchored to a model (bar/circle/number line), and stretch the language to name unit (1/b), proper (a<b), improper (a≥b) and mixed numbers so children meet the full grammar early rather than believing 'you can't have 5/4'.
bestPractices: Introduce numerator/denominator as JOBS ('how many equal parts in the whole' vs 'how many we took') tied to a shaded model, not as memorised top/bottom labels
Say the fraction as a quantity ('three-quarters') and read the symbol together, so 3/4 is heard as one number, never 'three, four'
Deliberately include improper and mixed forms (5/4, 1 1/4) so children learn the notation can name amounts greater than one
Contrast unit and non-unit fractions (1/4 vs 3/4) and classify examples so the words attach to structure
Link symbol, spoken words and diagram three ways (write it, say it, shade it) and back again
keyRepresentations: Bar/area model with the symbol written alongside and each number labelled to its job
Number line locating the fraction as a single point (a fraction is a number)
Fraction wall showing unit vs non-unit and proper vs improper
commonMisconceptions: Reads 3/4 as two separate whole numbers ('three, four') rather than one quantity
Writes the fraction upside down — swaps numerator and denominator
Believes an improper fraction like 5/4 or 4/3 'isn't a real number / can't exist'
Mixes the vocabulary — calls the bottom number the numerator
Thinks 2/4 and 1/2 must be different amounts because the numbers differ

learn.summary: Fraction notation a/b is a compact language naming a SINGLE number: the denominator says how many equal parts one whole is split into, and the numerator counts how many of those parts we have. Teach the vocabulary in use, always anchored to a model (bar, circle, number line), and deliberately stretch the language to name unit (1/b), proper (a<b), improper (a>=b) and mixed numbers so children meet the full grammar early rather than believing 'you can't have 5/4'. A proposed emphasis is on GENERATING notation (shade N of M equal parts and watch the symbol form) so the symbol is tied to an amount, rather than only memorising top/bottom labels.

activities.title: Build the fraction, build the name
feedback: If a learner reads 5/4 as impossible, have them collect five quarter-pieces one at a time and watch the pile pass one whole and land at 1 1/4; then place that point on a number line beyond 1 so it is visibly one number.

If a learner writes the symbol upside down (for example 8/3 for 'three of eight slices'), have them re-shade and write bottom-first: 'How many equal parts in the whole? That is the bottom. How many did we take? That is the top.'
If a learner says 2/4 and 1/2 must differ because the numbers differ, return to the overlay: same shaded length, two names.
If a learner is unsure whether a unit fraction like 1/4 is unit or proper, confirm it is both a proper fraction and specifically a unit fraction, so it goes in the unit tray.
Optional: let the symbol N/M write itself above the bar as the dial and shade controls change, and let a voice name each number to its job, so the link between action and symbol is immediate.
activities.rationale: Writing, saying and shading the notation together, and seeing the symbol respond to the amount, may consolidate the vocabulary and the parts-of-one-whole meaning. Deliberately including improper and mixed forms targets the documented belief that an improper fraction is not a number, and the overlay targets treating numerator and denominator as separate numbers.
sourceClaims: A facet of poor fraction understanding is focusing on numerators and denominators as separate numbers rather than a single number; and many students believe an improper fraction such as four-thirds is not a number.
Year 2/3 pupils name and write fractions, recognise unit and non-unit fractions and fractions greater than one; fraction vocabulary is a national-curriculum expectation.
learnerActions: Cut a bar into M equal parts (for example set it to 4) and shade N of them (for example 3), then write the symbol that matches: the parts taken on top, the equal parts in one whole on the bottom.
As you shade, say the fraction as one spoken quantity ('three-quarters'), not 'three, four'.
Label each number to its job: the numerator is 'the 3 parts we took' and the denominator is 'the 4 equal parts in one whole'.

Now push the numerator past the denominator (shade 5 parts when the whole holds 4): the shading overflows into a second whole. Record that this is called an improper fraction (5/4) and write its mixed twin beside it (1 1/4).

Sort every fraction you build into four trays: unit (numerator 1 and denominator more than 1, like 1/4), proper-but-not-unit (numerator more than 1 but less than the denominator, like 3/4), improper (numerator as big as or bigger than the denominator, like 5/4 or 4/4; 1/1 also goes here because it equals one whole), and mixed (like 1 1/4). A unit fraction like 1/4 is a special kind of proper fraction, so sort each card into its most specific tray.

Shade 2/4 of a bar, then slide that shaded length to overlay 1/2 of a bar of the same length (the same whole): notice the symbols differ but the shaded length is identical, so they name the same amount.
activities.intendedInsight: Fraction notation names one number. The bottom number tells how many equal parts one whole is cut into; the top counts how many we have. Pushing the numerator past the denominator shows 5/4 is a real number greater than one (equal to 1 1/4), and overlaying 2/4 on 1/2 shows different symbols can name the same quantity.

activities.title: Label the fraction's jobs
feedback: If a learner mixes the vocabulary (calls the bottom number the numerator), reconnect each number to its job on the shaded model before naming it.
If a learner reads the symbol as two separate numbers, read symbol to word to shaded amount as one quantity several times ('three-quarters').
activities.rationale: A clear labelled reference reinforces naming and the parts-of-one-whole meaning. This is a naming and reading scaffold; on its own it does not let a child build improper or mixed forms or manipulate equivalence, so pair it with the builder.
sourceClaims: Year 2/3 pupils name and write fractions, recognise unit and non-unit fractions and fractions greater than one; fraction vocabulary is a national-curriculum expectation.
learnerActions: Look at 3/4 beside its shaded bar. Point to the numerator and say what it does ('the parts we took'); point to the denominator and say what it does ('the equal parts in one whole').
Point to the whole bar and explain it is the one whole that was cut up.
Answer the prompt 'What if the top number were bigger than the bottom?' and predict what the picture and the name would become.
Link the three forms both directions: write the symbol, say the words, shade the picture, and go back again.
activities.intendedInsight: Each part of the written symbol has a fixed job tied to the model, and the symbol, spoken words and diagram are three views of the same single quantity.

activities.title: Classify and match for fluency
feedback: Correct classification requires a reason: ask 'How do you know this is improper?' and expect 'the top is as big as or bigger than the bottom, so it is one whole or more.'

If matching or filling in is correct but the learner still cannot read 5/4 as one quantity greater than one, return to the builder and number line, because recognition and fluency practice alone does not by itself elicit construction of the single-number idea.
activities.rationale: Classification and matching assess fluency with the four fraction types and the vocabulary. They check recall and recognition; a sort or match can check that the vocabulary attaches to structure but does not by itself elicit the building and explaining that construct the single-number understanding, so use them after the building work.
sourceClaims: Year 2/3 pupils name and write fractions, recognise unit and non-unit fractions and fractions greater than one; fraction vocabulary is a national-curriculum expectation.
learnerActions: Sort a set of fraction cards into unit, proper, improper and mixed, giving one example of each; remember a unit fraction (numerator 1, denominator more than 1, like 1/4) is a special kind of proper fraction, so place it in the unit tray and keep the proper tray for proper fractions whose numerator is greater than 1 (a card such as 1/1 equals one whole and goes in the improper tray).
Match spoken words to written symbols (for example 'three-quarters' to 3/4).
Fill in the missing number: a shaded picture shows ?/? parts; write both the numerator and the denominator.
Explain in your own words why 2/4 and 1/2 are equivalent.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure classification and word-symbol matching show the vocabulary has attached to structure, not just to top/bottom positions.

constraints: Always anchor the vocabulary to a model (bar, circle or number line); do not teach numerator/denominator as memorised top/bottom labels.
Deliberately include improper and mixed forms (5/4, 1 1/4) so children learn the notation can name amounts greater than one; do not leave them believing 'you can't have 5/4'.
Say fractions as single spoken quantities ('three-quarters') so the symbol is heard as one number, never 'three, four'.

When sorting into unit / proper / improper / mixed, make clear that a unit fraction is a special proper fraction (sort it as unit) so the categories are not treated as if a fraction like 1/4 belonged in two trays.

The labelled-reference activity supports naming and reading only; it cannot let a child build improper/mixed forms or manipulate equivalence, so it is a scaffold, not a replacement for generating notation.

Classification, matching and fill-in tasks check fluency and recognition; a sort or match does not itself elicit independent construction of the single-number idea, so follow them with building and explaining.

A spoken quiz or dialogue can check naming, but it does not by itself elicit the writing and shading that produce the notation; pair any dialogue with building rather than treating talk as a substitute.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and no comparative efficacy of the builder over the reference or fluency tasks is claimed.

The legacy row dismissed a third dimension with a banked 'flat concept rendered in 3D isn't 3D' rule. That is a catalog-style universal claim not established by the cited sources; it has been dropped. Fraction notation is planar symbol-and-model work, so a 3D rendering has no clear affordance here, but no universal impossibility is asserted.

Self-audit of worked values: a bar cut into 4 equal parts with 5 parts shaded gives 5/4 = 1 1/4 (one whole and one quarter) - correct. 2/4 and 1/2 name the same length - correct. 3 of 8 equal slices is 3/8, and the upside-down error 8/3 is flagged as the error to fix, never presented as acceptable.

The diagnostic reasoning that the bottom number being bigger than the top tells us the fraction is less than one whole is sound for positive fractions and is retained as reasoning behind classification. Note this compares a fixed structure (top vs bottom within one symbol) and does not involve any denominator rule 'flipping'.

The original four-way sort treated 'unit' and 'proper' as separate trays, but every unit fraction (numerator 1) is also a proper fraction. The activities now state that a unit fraction is a special proper fraction and is sorted into the unit tray, removing the double-placement ambiguity.
Original probeDeeper content (e.g. eating all 8 slices gives 8/8 = 1) is a useful extension not fully expanded into an activity here; it can be added when the builder reaches a full whole.

probeDeeper: You wrote 3/8. If you had eaten all 8 slices, what fraction is that, and what number does it equal?
Someone writes 4/3 and says 'that's impossible — you can't split 4 things into 3'. What would you tell them?
Why does the bottom number being bigger than the top tell us the fraction is less than one whole?
Is 2/4 a different amount from 1/2, or the same? How do the numbers show it?
assess.correctAnswer: Writes 3/8; says the bottom number 8 (denominator) is the number of equal slices the whole pizza was cut into and the top number 3 (numerator) is how many of those slices were eaten. Reads 5/4 as 'five-quarters' (five-fourths), explains it means five parts each a quarter, which is more than one whole (one whole and one more quarter, 1 1/4), and yes it is allowed — an improper fraction is still a single number.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the symbol as two separate whole numbers — '3/8' becomes 'three, eight' rather than one quantity, three-eighths
errorPatterns.nextMove: Locate the fraction as one point on a number line and say it as one word ('three-eighths'); repeatedly read symbol→word→shaded amount as a single quantity
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the numbers aloud separately, or compares fractions by looking at numerator and denominator independently, never naming a single amount

errorPatterns.pattern: Writes the fraction upside down — puts the number of parts taken on the bottom (numerator and denominator swapped)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reconnect each number to its job on a shaded model ('how many equal parts in the whole? that's the bottom'); write the symbol WHILE shading, bottom-first
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 8/3 for 'three of eight slices', or shades correctly but records the symbol reversed

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes an improper fraction isn't a real number — '5/4 isn't allowed, you can't have five quarters / four thirds'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build 5/4 by collecting five quarter-pieces; show it passes one whole and equals 1 1/4; place it on a number line beyond 1 so it is visibly a single number
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Refuses to read 5/4, calls it a mistake, or tries to 'fix' it to 4/5

responseLevels.gap: Reads 3/8 as 'three, eight' and cannot say which number is the numerator/denominator or swaps them; says 5/4 'isn't allowed'.
responseLevels.full: Uses the vocabulary fluently in context, writes 3/8 with each number justified as parts-of-one-whole, reads and interprets 5/4 as one number greater than one (1 1/4), and classifies unit/proper/improper/mixed correctly.
responseLevels.partial: Names numerator and denominator and writes 3/8 correctly in the pizza context, but treats the two numbers as separate counts — cannot read 5/4 as a single quantity greater than one, and cannot reliably classify unit/proper/improper/mixed.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a pizza cut into 8 equal slices, and you eat 3 of them. Write that as a fraction, and as you write it tell me what each number in it stands for. Then I have written 5/4 on the board for a recipe — read it aloud for me and tell me what it means, and whether writing a fraction like that is allowed.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has only memorised 'top and bottom' can still parrot the labels, but two moves separate real notation understanding from label-recall: reading 5/4 as a single quantity greater than one (vs 'you can't do that') exposes the belief that improper fractions aren't numbers, and justifying 3 and 8 as parts-of-one-whole (vs reading '3/8' as 'three, eight') exposes the separate-whole-numbers facet.
